question_text: Draw a high-side current sensing circuit. Why can't we make the shunt resistor incredibly large to get a massive, easy-to-read voltage signal? Conversely, why can't we make it incredibly small to eliminate power loss? What specific Op-Amp datasheet spec dictates this lower limit?
answer_text: Too large causes excessive power loss and load voltage drop. Too small causes the signal to be completely buried by the op-amp's "Input Offset Voltage" (V_os) spec.
explanation_text:
1. Too Large: The resistor will burn massive heat (P = I^2 * R). Additionally, it causes a significant voltage drop (V = I * R), meaning your load receives less voltage than intended (e.g., a 5V supply dropping to 4V before hitting the load).
2. Too Small: If the resistor is extremely small, the voltage drop might only be 0.5mV. Every op-amp has an imperfection called Input Offset Voltage (V_os)—a tiny artificial DC error voltage (e.g., 1mV to 3mV) inherently built into the input pins. If your real signal is 0.5mV and the op-amp's internal V_os error is 1mV, your current measurement is completely corrupted and useless. You must choose a shunt large enough so the voltage drop completely dominates the V_os spec.
bonus_question_text: Aside from Input Offset Voltage, what other environmental factor severely limits how small your shunt resistor can be?
bonus_answer_text: Electromagnetic Interference (EMI) and noise. A tiny 0.5mV signal is easily swallowed by background AC noise or switching ripples on the PCB.
